newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU says aims to cut fish catch, not jobs or fleet.
newsitem.headline: EU says aims to cut fish catch, not jobs or fleet.

text.p: European Fisheries Commissioner Emma Bonino, facing a fierce fight over plans to combat chronic overfishing, said on Thursday that catches, not boats or jobs, would be cut by up to 40 percent over six years.
Bonino appeared to row back from a proposal in May calling for significant reductions in the capacity of trawler fleets hunting seriously endangered fish stocks.

"There has been a misunderstanding," Bonino told a news conference. "The Commission is accused of wishing to break up 40 percent of our fleets, sacrificing jobs and means of production that could be used when stocks have recovered."
"That's false," the Italian EU commissioner stressed.
"Brussels is also accused of wiping out 40 percent of (fishing industry) jobs. That's also wrong," Bonino said.
The aim was to cut catches for only the most endangered stocks such as cod, haddock, sardines and salmon, she said.
It did not mean a 40 percent reduction in the fleet, she said, noting that for some stocks, such as tropical tuna and Baltic herring and sprat, no cuts were envisaged.

However Bonino acknowledged there would be some job losses. "I do think we need a partial reduction of the fleet," she said, explaining this was the best way to achieve a permanent reduction in fishing capacity.
Bonino said that the May proposal, which suggested a combination of cuts in time at sea and fleet size, may have been mistranslated or not clearly expressed.
Bonino said consultations with 60 regional fishing groups and member governments had at least found agreement on overfishing though there were wide differences over its cure.

The Commission was ready to help, she said. "We believe that market forces alone would impose a law of the jungle leading to an unequal decimation of fleets and above all a decimation of stocks which could never be reversed."

In June the Commission's proposal was attacked by EU fisheries ministers with Britain insisting that the EU must first deal with "quota hoppers" -- boats from one EU state which register in another so as to take part of that country's quota.
In Britain some 150 boats, mainly Spanish and Dutch vessels, are registered and take 20 percent of the national quota.

Bonino said that British fishermen wishing to lay up their vessels could now obtain EU aid and would no longer need to sell their licences to foreigners. But the British government must continue to provide matching funds.
Other countries said the Commission's proposed cuts were excessive and would cause unaccepable jobs losses in coastal communities with little other prospect of employment.
Bonino recognised that the changes would be painful. But she pointed out that small, inshore vessels, which account for 70 percent of the EU fishing fleet, were exempted from the cuts.
EU aid amounting to 460 million Ecus ($575 million) or a total of 2.8 billion Ecus ($3.5 billion) was available between 1994-99 to ease the restructuring, she added.

EU fisheries ministers are expected to renew their attack on the proposals at a meeting in Luxembourg on Monday. But Ireland, which holds the EU presidency, hopes that political guidelines will be given so that agreement can be reached in November.
